## Why This Topic Matters

Causal inference defines the contrast of interest and the assumptions needed to learn it from observed data.

## Learning Objectives

- interpret the R workflow and its output; and
- adapt the examples to a related analysis.

## Learning Material

#### Causal inference and association regression

<!-- generated-learning-note -->
This section develops **Causal inference and association regression**. Read the model specification together with its assumptions and the scale of each reported effect.


- Still need to consider the chronological order in design;
- Well designed observation study is suitable for causal inference;
- Generally associated analysis estimate is larger or smaller than the causal inference; 
- Associated analysis is used for strata and it is hard to deal with interaction (with exposure) and noncollapsibility so CI should be recommended;
- Data imputation is also needed;
- Double robust estimate is more robust;
- Bootstrapping sampling should be more than 80% with more than 1000 samples and the statistic is not necessarily normal distribution;
- Categorizing should be based on the special knowledge not quartile/tertile/ ROC/ ;
- Ltmle longitudinal study should be less than 30 times measurements; 
- Nonparameter method has fewer assumptions but is computation resource consuming (sometimes less precise); 
- The distribution will be changed after normalization;

#### Why RCT is gold standard

<!-- generated-learning-note -->
This subsection explains **Why RCT is gold standard** and shows how it contributes to the overall Causal inference and associated regression workflow.


In a randomized control trial (RCT) we assume [that](https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/308397/why-is-average-treatment-effect-different-from-average-treatment-effect-on-the-t). 

$$
\mathrm{E}[Y^0|D=1] = \mathrm{E}[Y^0|D=0]
$$
and
$$
\mathrm{E}[Y^1|D=1] = \mathrm{E}[Y^1|D=0]
$$


Since
$$
\begin{align}
\mathrm{E}[\delta] =& \{ \pi \mathrm{E}[Y^1|D=1] + (1-\pi) \mathrm{E}[Y^1|D=0] \} \\ -& \{ \pi \mathrm{E}[Y^0|D=1] + (1-\pi) \mathrm{E}[Y^0|D=0] \}=ATE
\end{align}
$$

then

$$
\mathrm{E}[Y^1|D=1] - \mathrm{E}[Y^0|D=0]=ATE
$$

```{.r .cell-code}
#' Using the bootstrap to obtain confidence intervals 
bootfunc <- function(data,index){
  boot_dat <- data[index,]
  model0 <- glm(modelForm,data=subset(boot_dat,qsmk==0),family=binomial("logit"))
  model1 <- glm(modelForm,data=subset(boot_dat,qsmk==1),family=binomial("logit"))
  mu1 <- predict(model1,newdata=boot_dat,type="response")
  mu0 <- predict(model0,newdata=boot_dat,type="response")
  
  marg_stand_OR_ <- (mean(mu1)/mean(1-mu1))/(mean(mu0)/mean(1-mu0))
  marg_stand_RR_ <- mean(mu1)/mean(mu0)
  marg_stand_RD_ <- mean(mu1)-mean(mu0)
  res <- c(marg_stand_RD_,marg_stand_RR_,marg_stand_OR_)
  return(res)
}

#' Run the boot function. Set a seed to obtain reproducibility
set.seed(123)
boot_res <- boot(nhefs,bootfunc,R=2000)
```

#### Double robust estimation- 1

<!-- generated-learning-note -->
This subsection explains **Double robust estimation- 1** and shows how it contributes to the overall Causal inference and associated regression workflow.

**Purpose.** This block carries out the next computational step in the workflow. Track the objects it creates and how they are used by later steps.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# using the sl3 function create the super learner, that contains a simple
# average estimator and a glm estimator.
lrnr_glm <- make_learner(Lrnr_glm)
lrnr_mean <- make_learner(Lrnr_mean)
sl <- Lrnr_sl$new(learners = list(lrnr_glm,lrnr_mean))

learner_list <- list(Y = sl, A = sl)

# PREPARE THE THINGS WE WANT TO FEED IN TO TMLE3
# ate_spec defines the exposure levels we want 
# to compare
ate_spec <- tmle_ATE(treatment_level = 1, control_level = 0)

# nodes define the variables we want to adjsut for, and the exposure and the outcome
nodes <- list(W = c("sex", "age", "income", "sbp", "dbp", "price71", "tax71", "race"), 
              A = "qsmk", 
              Y = "wt_delta")

# Run the tmle3 function using the pieces defined above 
tmle_fit <- tmle3(ate_spec, nhefs, nodes, learner_list)
```

## Interpreting the Results

State the target estimand, causal structure, exchangeability assumptions, positivity, and consistency before fitting a model. Treat the output as evidence generated under the stated data, coding choices, and assumptions. Before using the workflow in practice, replace example inputs with validated data and confirm that the method targets the intended scientific question.

## Key Takeaways

- **Connect method to purpose.** Identify the question and target quantity before choosing code or a model.
- **Read code and output together.** Confirm what each object, estimate, interval, table, or plot represents.
- **Check assumptions and diagnostics.** A successful computation is not by itself evidence that the result is reliable.
- **Adapt deliberately.** When applying the example elsewhere, document changes to data definitions, parameters, and analytical choices.
